keep.brief: Hellion (Terran, Factory, t2), with the Hellbat as its second mode by the modes rule: cover the fast buggy's line of flame against Light units and the Hellbat form (slower, tougher, a short wide cone of flame, Biological so Medivacs heal it), switched both ways once an Armory stands (transform, fast-and-tough variant); the Factory can also build it as a Hellbat, but the base form stays the Hellion; ignore the co-op values in the infobox.

keep.brief: Widow Mine (Terran, Factory, t2): cover the small robot that digs in and is itself the mine (lay-mines, be-the-mine variant; its own burrow, not the Zerg research), the one heavy splash missile at the first enemy in range, the long reload, and whether it stays hidden while reloading at 5.0.17 (Drilling Claws or the Concealment upgrade).

keep.brief: Siege Tank (Terran, Factory with tech lab, t2): cover the light gun of tank mode and the locked-down siege mode (deploy-siege-mode, siege-gun variant), siege mode's minimum range, splash that also hurts friends, and a reach longer than its own sight (spotter hook); it is the game's price anchor (525), so show the band arithmetic.

keep.brief: Cyclone (Terran, Factory with tech lab, t2): cover Lock On, which ties its guns to one ground or air target and keeps them firing by themselves while it drives, until the timer ends or the target escapes the leash (tether-to-target, proposed); 5.0.12 reworked it and 5.0.14 restored the 5.0.11 version, so check which version each page describes.

keep.brief: Thor (Terran, Factory with tech lab and Armory, t3): cover the heavy ground cannons and the anti-air choice between splash missiles for swarms of light fliers and single heavy shells for big ships (switch-weapon-mode, spread-or-focus variant), the delay of the switch that Smart Servos shortens, and its Massive attribute.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Read the enemy's air mix and pick the matching mode; the spread-or-focus variant's example.

keep.brief: Viking (Terran, Starport, t2; built in Fighter mode, its base form): cover the long-range air-to-air missiles, landing as a ground walker with a gun of its own (transform, ground-and-air variant), each form hitting only its own layer, and its exposure to anti-air while it changes.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The ground-and-air transform built around out-ranging other fliers.

keep.brief: Medivac (Terran, Starport, t2): cover the seats for infantry or one vehicle (carry-passengers, dropship and airlift variants), healing that reaches living units only, never machines (repair-allies), the afterburner boost (dash, sprint variant), and the 5.0.16b revert of loading nearby units.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Carry-and-heal support whose healing depends on what the patient is made of.

keep.brief: Liberator (Terran, Starport, t2): cover the splash air-to-air missiles and Defender Mode, which anchors it in the sky over a chosen ground circle where any ground unit takes heavy single shots (deploy-siege-mode, zone-anchor variant); Advanced Ballistics at the Fusion Core adds reach.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A no-go circle cast from the air; the zone-anchor variant's example.

keep.brief: Raven (Terran, Starport with tech lab, t2): an unarmed flying detector; cover the short-lived Auto-Turret (deploy-turret, timed-drop variant), Interference Matrix, which shuts down one mechanical or Psionic unit and needs research since 5.0.12 (disable-machine, weapons-lock variant), and the missile that lowers armour in an area (mark-target, an id with no unit yet); code the ability set left after patches 4.0 and 4.1.4.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The unarmed caster: disable, drop a gun, weaken for the team; the first unit for mark-target.

keep.brief: Banshee (Terran, Starport with tech lab, t2): cover the gunship that hits only ground targets and the researched Cloaking Field that burns energy while it is on (cloak, cloak-on-key and fire-from-cloak variants), plus the Hyperflight Rotors speed research.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A cloak with a time limit that forces the enemy to invest in detection.

keep.brief: Battlecruiser (Terran, Starport with tech lab and Fusion Core, t3): cover firing while moving, the jump anywhere on the map after a delay in which it can still be hit (teleport), and the Yamato Cannon after Weapon Refit (fire-power-shot, wind-up-shot variant); Massive.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Map-wide repositioning with a vulnerable wind-up, and the registry's fire-power-shot example.

keep.brief: Zergling (Zerg, Larva once a Spawning Pool stands, t1): cover the two bodies per purchase, the fast melee swarm (Metabolic Boost) and the one-way morph into the Baneling (upgrade-in-field, morph-up variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The cheapest swarm body count and the morph-up variant's example.

keep.brief: Baneling (Zerg, morphed from a Zergling with a Baneling Nest, t1): cover the rolling acid bomb that dies to splash Light units without hurting friends (self-destruct), waiting burrowed as a living mine and going off from below (burrow, tripwire-ambush; self-destruct, buried-trap), the toggle that lets it attack buildings, and a price that counts the Zergling's share.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Cheap mass suicide splash and the buried ambush; the registry's self-destruct example.

keep.brief: Roach (Zerg, Larva with Roach Warren, t1): cover the cheap, tough ranged brute, its fast healing while burrowed (heal-self; burrow, mend-below) and crawling underground after Tunneling Claws (burrow, tunnel); Burrow itself is side-wide research.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Burrow to heal and tunnel past defences, answered only by detection.

keep.brief: Ravager (Zerg, morphed from a Roach, t1): cover Corrosive Bile, a blob that lands on a chosen spot after a visible delay, hits ground and air there and breaks Force Fields, on a short cooldown (bombard-area, called-strike variant); its price counts the Roach.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A dodgeable skill-shot bombard on a cheap frontline unit.

keep.brief: Hydralisk (Zerg, Larva with Hydralisk Den, t2): cover the fragile, hard-hitting attack on ground and air, the Lunge burst researched since 5.0.14 (dash) and the one-way morph into the Lurker (upgrade-in-field).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The glass cannon that needs protecting.

keep.brief: Lurker (Zerg, morphed from a Hydralisk with a Lurker Den, t2): cover attacking only while burrowed, the spines driven along a line that hit everything in it (burrow, buried-strike; deploy-siege-mode), and staying unseen until detected; it burrows without the Burrow research.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The hidden zone holder: dig in and the ground ahead is lethal.

keep.brief: Queen (Zerg, Hatchery with a Spawning Pool, not from Larva, t1): cover Transfusion on living units and buildings (repair-allies), Creep Tumors that spread the Zerg's fast ground (spread-favoured-ground, proposed), Inject Larva on a Hatchery (boost-production, proposed), its reach to fliers, and its speed on and off creep.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Team-economy support and ground your own side spreads; source of two proposed ids.

keep.brief: Overlord (Zerg, Larva, t1): cover the unarmed, very slow flier whose life raises the Zerg supply cap (raise-team-cap, proposed), the creep it can drip below itself (spread-favoured-ground), seats bought one Overlord at a time with Mutate Ventral Sacs (carry-passengers; upgrade-in-field) and the morph into the Overseer; no role may fit cleanly, so add a fit note.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A unit whose value is the team's cap, not its combat; killing it stalls production.

keep.brief: Overseer (Zerg, morphed from an Overlord at Lair, t2): cover detection, Spawn Changeling (disguise, look-like-their-own variant; the Changeling is coded here), the slime that stops an enemy building from producing for a while (stall-structure, proposed) and Oversight Mode, which stops it to see farther (a sight variant of deploy-siege-mode); it still provides supply.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Spy decoys and stalled buildings.

keep.brief: Mutalisk (Zerg, Larva with Spire, t2): cover the fast flying harasser whose glaive bounces on to two more targets (weapon trait chain) and its regeneration, faster than other Zerg (armour model self-repair).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The bouncing attack and hit-and-run by regeneration.

keep.brief: Corruptor (Zerg, Larva with Spire, t2): cover the air-only attack with a bonus against Massive targets, Caustic Spray on buildings whose damage climbs the longer it is held (channel-ramping-damage, proposed) and the one-way morph into the Brood Lord.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A dedicated counter to capital ships, with a structure-only side job.

keep.brief: Brood Lord (Zerg, morphed from a Corruptor with a Greater Spire, t3): cover the slow flying siege beast whose shots hatch short-lived Broodlings that attack ground units and block them (weapon family drone-launcher; the Broodling is coded here), its long ground-only reach and its helplessness against anti-air; the price counts the Corruptor; check the 5.0.15 hotfix speed change.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Attacks that spawn blockers; an air siege unit with no answer to anti-air.

keep.brief: Infestor (Zerg, Larva with Infestation Pit, t2), unarmed at 5.0.17: cover moving while burrowed, Fungal Growth (a heavy slow with damage that also reveals hidden units and blocks blinks, jumps, burrowing and boarding: snare-in-area, proposed), Neural Parasite, which borrows one enemy while it channels (mind-control, leashed-parasite variant), and Microbial Shroud, which cuts ranged damage on friends below it (rally-allies); its infobox still lists infested terrans, removed in 4.11.0.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Crowd control, borrowing an enemy through a tether, and cover for allies.

keep.brief: Swarm Host (Zerg, Larva with Infestation Pit, t2): cover the weaponless host that, on a long cooldown, releases a pair of free, short-lived Locusts that fly over terrain and land to attack (launch-drones, timed-wave variant; the Locust is coded here); campaign strains are out.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The registry's ability example for launch-drones: attrition by free timed minions from far away.

keep.brief: Viper (Zerg, Larva with Hive, t3), an unarmed flying caster: cover Abduct, which yanks one unit to it (pull-target, ally-rescue variant), Blinding Cloud, which cuts enemy ground ranged units down to melee reach (lay-smoke, blinding-cloud variant), Parasitic Bomb on a flier that hurts the fliers around it (infest-vehicle, contagion variant) and Consume, which drains a friendly building for energy (consume-ally-for-energy, proposed; compare sacrifice-for-allies, feed-the-caster variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Pulls and range denial; the registry's pull-target example.

keep.brief: Ultralisk (Zerg, Larva with Ultralisk Cavern, t3): cover the huge melee beast whose blades cleave through crowds, its immunity to slows, stuns and mind control (immune links), no reach to fliers, and its Massive attribute.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Crowd-control immunity as a defining trait.

keep.brief: Zealot (Protoss, Gateway or warp-in, t1): cover the shielded melee warrior and Charge after Twilight Council research, which closes the gap fast (dash with delivery ram); recharging shields and warp-in at a power field are game-wide.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The gap-closing charge; the registry's dash example.

keep.brief: Stalker (Protoss, Gateway with Cybernetics Core, t1): cover the fast ranged walker that hits ground and air with a bonus against Armored, and Blink after research, a short instant jump to chase, escape, cross cliffs or pull a hurt Stalker back (teleport, short-blink variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The short tactical blink; the short-blink variant's example.

keep.brief: Sentry (Protoss, Gateway with Cybernetics Core, t1): cover Force Field walls that block movement (build-cover, energy-wall variant), Guardian Shield, which cuts ranged damage near it (rally-allies, ward-aura variant), and Hallucination copies for scouting and feints (spawn-decoy, an id with no unit yet); campaign abilities are out.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Walls and decoys that shape the field; the first unit for spawn-decoy.

keep.brief: Adept (Protoss, Gateway with Cybernetics Core, t1): cover the bonus against Light and Psionic Transfer, an untouchable shade it steers and then jumps to unless it calls it off (teleport, projected-image variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The feint teleport: commit, or cancel and keep the enemy guessing.

keep.brief: High Templar (Protoss, Gateway with Templar Archives, t3): cover Psionic Storm, which hurts every unit in an area over a few seconds, friends included (leave-hazard-zone, ranged-storm variant), Feedback, which empties a target's energy and damages it by that amount (burn-energy, proposed), and the merge of two Templar into an Archon (merge-into-unit, proposed); take the Storm figure from Blizzard's 5.0.15 hotfix and 5.0.17 notes, not the wiki.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Area denial with friendly fire, energy burn and merging.

keep.brief: Dark Templar (Protoss, Gateway with Dark Shrine, t3): cover the melee assassin that is always invisible (sensor trait stealth, not a cloak key), Shadow Stride after research (teleport) and the merge into an Archon (merge-into-unit).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). Permanent stealth and a hard detection check.

keep.brief: Archon (Protoss, made only by merging two High or Dark Templar, t3): cover the body that is almost all recharging shield, the splash on ground and air with a bonus against Biological, its Massive attribute (it takes 4 transport slots) and a price that counts both Templar; the class is a guess for a floating energy being, so add a fit note.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The merged unit and a body that is nearly all shield.

keep.brief: Observer (Protoss, Robotics Facility, t2): cover the tiny, always-cloaked flying detector (stealth and detector traits) and Surveillance Mode, which parks it to see farther and since 5.0.15 gives it away (a sight variant of deploy-siege-mode).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The stealth scout with a stop-to-see-farther trade.

keep.brief: Warp Prism (Protoss, Robotics Facility, t2): cover the seats it fills from a short distance (carry-passengers) and Phasing Mode, a stationary power field where Gateway units warp in beside it (host-spawn-point, deployed-station and factory-relay variants).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The registry's host-spawn-point example: a mobile forward spawn point the enemy must hunt.

keep.brief: Immortal (Protoss, Robotics Facility, t2): cover the walker built to kill armour and Barrier, which springs up once it is hit and soaks damage for a few seconds, blocking the triggering hit too since 5.0.12 (raise-shield, an id with no unit yet); the campaign's Hardened Shields is out.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The reactive emergency shield; the first unit for raise-shield.

keep.brief: Colossus (Protoss, Robotics Facility with Robotics Bay, t3): cover the towering walker that strides up and down cliffs (mobility trait climb), the beam swept along a line through Light units, and its exposure to anti-air as if it flew (a likely target-types fit note).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A ground unit that counts as both ground and air when targeted.

keep.brief: Disruptor (Protoss, Robotics Facility with Robotics Bay, t3), unarmed at 5.0.17: cover Purification Nova, a ball it releases and steers for a moment before it bursts, wiping out a clump and hurting friends (steer-delayed-blast, proposed, or a fire-power-shot variant); the class is a guess for a floating robot sphere, so add a fit note.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A steered, delayed blast that enemies survive by scattering.

keep.brief: Phoenix (Protoss, Stargate, t2): cover the fast fighter that hits only fliers and shoots on the move, and Graviton Beam, which lifts a ground unit and keeps both it and the Phoenix out of the fight (pull-target, lift-and-hold variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A lift that removes one enemy for a while at the cost of the lifter.

keep.brief: Void Ray (Protoss, Stargate, t2): cover the beam that hits ground and air and Prismatic Alignment, a timed mode with more damage against Armored and slower movement (overclock-self, slow-but-strong variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A timed power mode with a mobility price; the slow-but-strong variant's example.

keep.brief: Oracle (Protoss, Stargate, t2): cover the Pulsar Beam, which works only while switched on and drains energy each second (fuel-weapon-with-energy, proposed), the cloaked Stasis Ward that freezes enemies who come near (lock-in-stasis, stasis-trap variant; lay-mines) and Revelation, which keeps an area's enemies visible for a while (reveal-area, tracking-reveal variant).
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). An energy-fed weapon and stasis as a hidden trap; the registry's lock-in-stasis example.

keep.brief: Tempest (Protoss, Stargate with Fleet Beacon, t3): cover the air attack that outranges every other flier, with a bonus against Massive, its shorter ground attack, and its slowness and weakness up close; Disintegration is campaign and co-op only.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The extreme-range anti-capital artillery ship.

keep.brief: Carrier (Protoss, Stargate with Fleet Beacon, t3): cover the capital ship with no gun of its own that fights through Interceptors it launches and rebuilds for minerals (weapon family drone-launcher; the Interceptor is coded here; Build Interceptor needs a fit note), and the counter of killing the drones.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). A weapon made of expendable drones.

keep.brief: Mothership (Protoss, Nexus once a Fleet Beacon stands, t3, one per player): cover the active Cloaking Field over nearby friends but never itself (cloak, cloak-field variant), the recall that pulls units in an area to it (teleport, move-teammates variant) and Time Warp, which slows enemies in a zone (leave-hazard-zone, slow-field variant), all on cooldowns since 5.0.12; no Mothership Core since 4.0.
keep.why: The plan codes every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the workers (no trim). The one-per-side support flagship.

keep.brief: Elephant (UNSC, Captain Cutter only; Firebase, 400, 2 population, tech 0): cover the armoured truck that must deploy before it trains Marines, Hellbringers and Spartans at the front (host-spawn-point or produce-unit-in-field: settle it by the two summaries), the turret upgrade that works only while it is deployed (deploy-siege-mode) and the Twin Engine upgrade; check whether it carries troops in skirmish, since the game notes say no buildable unit carries others while its Halopedia page calls it a personnel carrier.
keep.why: The batch's only factory on wheels: a forward barracks the enemy must hunt, useful only once parked. It overlaps the kept Warp Prism's forward warp-in point; training at the front from a ground hull, and a gun that works only while deployed, are what it adds. Cutter's own unit.

keep.brief: Cyclops (UNSC, Sergeant Forge only; Firebase, 125, 1 population, tech 1): cover the cheap exosuit that fights only in melee and exists to wreck structures, the Repair Kit upgrade that mends buildings and ground vehicles (repair-allies), the speed upgrade, and no anti-air; settle walker against infantry by the classes rule; leave out the thrown debris, which only hidden text on the Halo Wars page mentions.
keep.why: A melee demolition suit for a base-assault game that can switch to field repairs; Forge's own unit and Halo Wars' second UNSC entry. Halo Wars 2's Cyclops (Shock Rounds, no repair kit) is not a candidate, so the line stays here once.

keep.brief: Arbiter (Covenant leader hero; free with the first Temple, 400 to buy again, one at a time, outside the population cap): cover the twin energy swords; Rage, in which the player steers him and he leaps onto chosen targets while the team's supplies drain every second (overclock-self; drain-team-funds, proposed, or a resource term); the Rage upgrades (healing per kill, a cheaper Rage, an attack aura for nearby allies: rally-allies, damage sent back at attackers: retaliate-on-hit, and a permanent cloak at the end: cloak); that he reaches aircraft only in Rage; leave the Gravity Lift off (a base feature by the game notes).
keep.why: A berserk mode paid from the team's wallet by the second: the clearest drain-team-funds case. His cloak overlaps the kept Dark Templar and his boost the Marine's Stimpack; the running cost is what is new. Halo Wars 2's Arbiter has no running cost, so the line stays here.

keep.brief: Prophet of Regret (Covenant leader hero; the same terms as the Arbiter): cover the anti-gravity throne (hover), the plasma cannons with a fuel rod upgrade, two Protector Sentinel escorts bought as an upgrade (launch-drones), the last upgrade that makes him an aircraft, and Cleansing, a beam from an orbiting ship that the player steers anywhere in his sight, burning everything under it including his own side but never him, while supplies drain (steer-orbital-beam and drain-team-funds, proposed); counter: a Vampire's stasis once he flies.
keep.why: A steered, sustained beam as an ultimate, and a hover unit that an upgrade lifts into the air. The kept Disruptor steers a ball that bursts once; this beam is held and driven, so both stay. Halo Wars 2 has no Prophet.

keep.brief: Brute Chieftain (Covenant leader hero; the same terms): cover the gravity hammer against heavy vehicles, the upgrades that add a stun, a charged swing that drags enemies to him (pull-target) and an area stun, the Temple line that he kills stunned infantry outright (execute-target), and Vortex, a spinning field that shreds whatever is near and blows up when he ends it, later pulling in more (leave-hazard-zone; detonate-on-release, proposed), his only way to hit aircraft, with its supply drain; this leader also swaps the Ghost for the Chopper (notes).
keep.why: Timing the release of a held vortex is new. His pull overlaps the kept Viper and Phoenix, and the vortex the Psionic Storm, so the release blast is what he adds. Halo Wars 2's nearest unit, Decimus's Warlord, is cut as the same hammer line without the vortex.

keep.brief: Vampire (Covenant; Summit, 250, 2 population, tech 2): cover the needle turret against aircraft, Stasis, which pins an enemy aircraft, the Stasis Drain upgrade, which heals the Vampire from the pinned target's health (drain-health, an id with no unit yet), the Stasis Bomb upgrade, which makes a drained aircraft burst with area damage instead of crashing (detonate-victim, proposed), its weakness against ground targets, and that a Spartan cannot take it.
keep.why: The batch's only drain-health carrier, and an air duel that punishes tight formations. Halo Wars 2 has no Vampire.

keep.brief: Hunter (Covenant; Hall, 250, 2 population, tech 1): cover the bonded pair of armoured giants whose fuel rod cannons answer vehicles, useless against aircraft and poor against infantry; the Bonded Shield, which deflects many shots, Spirit Bond, a big damage boost only while both of the pair live (bond-with-partner, proposed), and the Assault Beam; settle how the pair is crewed (one entry for two bodies); what a revived Hunter's bond does rests on hidden text, so leave it out.
keep.why: A unit built for two players: stronger together, so the enemy splits them to break it. band-together counts a group, not one named partner. Halo Wars 2's Hunters lost the bond, so the line stays here.

keep.brief: Banshee (Covenant; Summit, 200, 2 population, tech 1): cover the fastest unit in the game, a hovering flier armed with a fuel rod cannon and plasma cannons, its Boost (dash), the faster-firing cannon upgrade, and Sacrifice, after which a badly hurt Banshee tries to crash into ground targets for area damage (self-destruct, set off by low health); Wolverines and Vampires counter it.
keep.why: A death you can aim: the dying pilot steers the wreck into the enemy. The kept Baneling chooses to blow up and the kept Manhattan goes off wherever it falls; this one turns its last moment into a strike. Halo Wars 2's Banshee has no dive, so the line stays here.

keep.brief: Ghost (Covenant, for the Arbiter and the Prophet; Factory, 1 population, tech 0; 100 on the Factory table, 125 on its page): cover the cheap, fast anti-gravity bike that shreds infantry and folds against armour, Boosted Ram (dash with delivery ram), Strafe, which dodges most grenades and rockets (armour model evasive, new to the data), and the Scout Shield; picking up crates is game-wide, so leave it off.
keep.why: A dodge that beats slow projectiles, a natural fit for a shooter. Its ram repeats the kept Zealot's charge; the Strafe is what it adds. Halo Wars 2's Ghost has no Strafe, so the line stays here.

keep.brief: Jerome-092 (UNSC hero for Captain Cutter; Armory, tech 1, 300 supplies and 275 power, one hero, bought again rather than revived in multiplayer): cover the Magnum he starts with, the Spartan Slam that crosses ledges other ground units cannot and hurts what it lands near (leap), the Hijack upgrade, in which an EMP holds an enemy vehicle or aircraft still while he takes it and his death cancels the takeover (hijack-vehicle, pin-then-take variant), the stun around a vehicle he slams onto, boarding a friendly vehicle to boost it (join-ally-crew), and the level-2 Spartan Laser; Alice-130 and Douglas-042 differ only in that weapon, and the Halo Wars Spartan (three per army, outside the population cap) goes in notes.
keep.why: Boarding as a skill with counterplay: guard your armour with anti-infantry. Halopedia's Red Team page (Halo Wars 2 section) says these Spartans act almost as in Halo Wars but add the EMP hold, the Slam and the cancel on death, so the Spartan line stays here once. Jarmen Kell's ranged crew snipe and the Line Officer are the data's other carriers.

keep.brief: Jackrabbit (UNSC; Firebase, tech 0; 220 supplies and 15 power on the Firebase table but 350 and 15 on its page, so settle the price): cover the cheap, very fast scout with the grenade launcher it has carried in multiplayer since June 2017, undoing enemy captures (a fit note: capture points are a game-mode rule; the Raid II leader power is a commander-power source), and the upgrade that adds a support drone that repairs it, widens its sight, reveals cloaked enemies and shoots (launch-drones, bought as an add-on); crate pickup is game-wide.
keep.why: One lasting helper drone bought as an add-on keeps a fragile scout alive: the launch-drones case that R3 left only on cut units (Generals' vehicle drones). The kept Swarm Host covers the timed-wave variant instead. Halo Wars' UNSC scout was the Warthog, so the line is new here.

keep.brief: Kinsano's Cyclops (UNSC hero for Kinsano; Armory, tech 1, 300 supplies and 275 power, one hero): cover the twin flamers, the quickly recharging shield, and the wall of fire it draws across the ground that burns whatever crosses it, larger at the top upgrade (leave-hazard-zone, a hazard shaped as a line), and no anti-air; settle infantry power suit against walker by the classes rule; the death blast is Blitz only, and Kinsano's Hellcharge power adds a death effect (on_death notes).
keep.why: A hazard shaped as a line that cuts a lane in two; the kept High Templar's storm is a circle. It shares only the suit with Halo Wars' Cyclops, whose job (melee demolition and repair) differs.

keep.brief: Colossus (UNSC, Sergeant Johnson only, in place of the Scorpion at the Garage; tech 3, 750 supplies and 120 power): cover the heavy walker's two guns fired together, an autocannon that hits everything including aircraft and a railgun that reaches ground targets from very far (family railgun), and the Stomp upgrade, a shock that stuns and hurts enemy ground units close around it (ground-slam, proposed); the free Colossus drop is campaign only.
keep.why: The ground slam on a key, and the first railgun in the data. The kept Planetary Annihilation Atlas slams as its weapon, not on a key, and the kept Thor splits ground and air jobs by a mode switch where this one fires both at once. Halo Wars 2's UNSC tier-3 entry.

keep.brief: Scarab (Banished super unit, every leader but Voridus; War Council, tech 3, 2,000 supplies and 2,000 power, 40 population, up to three at once): cover the main beam and Thrasher missiles, crossing any terrain (mobility trait climb), the plasma shield that makes it untouchable for a few moments on a key (become-invulnerable), only fair results against aircraft, and up to three Skitterers riding it; Voridus's Volatile Scarab and the Halo Wars Scarab (two at once, no shield) go in notes.
keep.why: The boss walker a team buys for its big moment, with the classic short invulnerability on a key (the data's Aurora Bomber is untouchable only during its fast run). Halo Wars 2 adds the shield and the riders to the Halo Wars line, so the Scarab stays here once.

keep.brief: Skitterer (Banished, Colony only; an outpost unit unlocked by a leader power, tech 1, 150 supplies and 20 power): cover the cheap, fast light-beam scout walker that attaches to a friendly unit as a turret, adds to the host's health, keeps firing, rides along and is destroyed only with the host (rarely sooner), with the host's size setting how many fit (a Scarab three, a Hunter pair two, a Huragok one) and no way to detach (ride-on-ally, proposed); gathering crates is game-wide; settle crew and nature for a machine run by a colony of worms.
keep.why: Riding a teammate as an extra gun and armour plate is a strong team-play idea that no data unit has; join-ally-crew boards inside, one rider at a time. The kept Elemental rides on the outside without fighting from the host, so the two show the same new id from two sides.

keep.brief: Hunter Captain (Banished hero for Colony; War Council, tech 1, 300 supplies and 275 power, one hero): cover the slow, heavily armoured body, the Siphon beam that heals it as it hits (weapon trait heal-on-hit), the Taunt upgrade that makes nearby enemies attack only it (draw-fire, an id with no unit yet), Improved Taunt (wider, and taunted enemies hit softer) and Siphon Overcharge (an area attack).
keep.why: The taunting tank: the first unit for draw-fire, and a clear team role. Halo Wars' Hunters are a different unit (the bonded pair, kept there); Halo Wars 2's own Hunter pair is not a candidate.

keep.brief: Shroud (Banished, every leader; Apex, tech 2, 400 supplies and 60 power): cover the unarmed support flier with two modes that exclude each other: deployed, a cloak over nearby allies for a limited time (cloak, cloak-field variant), and otherwise a point defence that shoots down incoming projectiles aimed at it or its allies, two at a time (intercept-for-allies, proposed, or the interceptor model if a source shows it guarding only itself); detectors and big volleys are its counters; the Shipmaster's leader-point upgrade widens the cloak (commander-power).
keep.why: Hide the raid or shield it, never both. Its cloak field overlaps the kept Mothership's; the group point defence and the forced choice are new. Halo Wars has no Shroud.

keep.brief: Methane Wagon (Banished, Yapyap only; an outpost unit unlocked by a leader power, 300 supplies and 120 power; tier 1 on the outpost table, 0 on its page): cover the always-on methane cloud that makes nearby Grunts fight better and weakens enemies inside it (buff-and-curse-aura, proposed; rally-allies as the fallback), the lobbed kegs that start the same cloud elsewhere (weapon trait zone if they are its plain attack, leave-hazard-zone if on a key), the blast on death that hurts nearby enemies (death-blast), and its poor fighting record yet its edge over a Marauder through the cloud; class vehicle or hover (a modified Shadow).
keep.why: One cloud that helps one kind of teammate and hurts the enemy at once; the kept Sentry's Guardian Shield only helps friends. Halo Wars has no such unit.

keep.brief: Commander (shared; every player starts with one, gate Start of the match, t1, never bought, so no cost band): code the Imperial body and name the other body classes and the 76 shared-stat skins in notes; cover building the basic factories, turrets and the Teleporter (build-structure, deploy-turret and build-linked-exits by the abilities rule), repair and reclaim (repair-allies; gather-resources with a fit note), its own metal and energy income, its gun, anti-air and torpedo weapons, the Uber Cannon that fires only on its order for 10,000 energy from the side's pool (fire-power-shot; resource energy), its death blast (no harm to allies since June 2025), and the side losing when its last Commander dies in the default mode (lose-match-on-death, proposed, unless the notes call it a game-mode rule).
keep.why: The king piece and builder whose survival is the team's, and the registry's fire-power-shot example from this game. Its power shot overlaps the kept Battlecruiser's Yamato Cannon; the king-piece rule and the building are what is new.

keep.brief: SXX-1304 Laser Platform (shared; Orbital Factory, t2, 4,000 metal, very high): cover the orbital gunship that fires straight down at what lies below it (a short downward reach, splash, a shot every few seconds paid in energy from the side's pool), its target order (commanders, orbital defences, nukes and economy buildings first), being always visible, travel between planets, and that only weapons that reach orbit can hit it; the word lists have no orbital layer, so take the closest terms (aircraft) and add fit notes (strike-from-orbit, proposed).
keep.why: A separate layer above the fight that only anti-orbit weapons reach; nothing in the data or in StarCraft II sits there. The kept Bluehawk is its counter.

keep.brief: Bluehawk (shared; Advanced Bot Factory, t2, 700 metal, low): cover its three launchers: long-range homing missiles against ground and sea targets that ignore shields and go for defences and commanders first, a heavier missile for orbital targets only, and a third against orbit and air whose listed special target is the Unit Cannon's launched units (shoot-down-drops, proposed; confirm on the Unit Cannon page that this means pods in flight before coding it).
keep.why: The ground team's answer to the orbital layer and to drops, the counter to the kept SXX-1304 and Astraeus. No data unit reaches orbit or shoots down units in flight.

keep.brief: Atlas (shared titan; built in the field by an advanced fabricator, gate Titan, t3, 30,000 metal, very high): cover its 60,000 health, its only weapon, a ground slam every five seconds that hits everything in a wide ring around it and ignores shields (ground-slam, proposed; the aim model radial may already fit the ring), commanders first in its target list, walking the seabed (amphibious), no teleporter use, and its death blast (no harm to allies, aircraft or orbital units).
keep.why: A walking earthquake that wants enemies close, and Planetary Annihilation's titan tier. Its slam is a weapon; the kept Halo Wars 2 Colossus has the same idea on a key, so the slam counts once, as one proposed id carried by both.

keep.brief: Manhattan (shared; Advanced Vehicle Factory, t2, 8,000 metal, very high): cover the mobile nuke with 15,000 health, its huge death blast that also hurts its own side (death-blast; weapon trait friendly-fire), the order to set it off on a target (self-destruct), Manhattans setting each other off (from the old Fandom page: check that it still holds), its radar and its amphibious movement.
keep.why: Its death is the bomb: the enemy must stop it far away, and its owner must keep it away from their own army. The kept Baneling chooses to blow up; this one punishes whoever kills it nearby.

keep.brief: Astraeus (shared; Orbital Launcher, t1, 200 metal, very low): cover the unarmed, frail orbital lander that carries one land unit, or an air or naval fabricator, even the Commander, to another planet (carry-passengers with one seat, and no transport role by the notes; drop-in-from-above; travel-between-worlds, proposed); unlike most orbital units it is not always visible; the orbital-layer gap applies as for the SXX-1304.
keep.why: The hop between worlds: a one-seat ferry to another front. The kept Medivac and Warp Prism carry within one map; travel to another arena is new.

keep.brief: Icarus (shared; Air Factory, t1, 150 metal, very low): cover the slow flying solar plant that adds energy to its side for as long as it lives (generate-income with a fit note, since that pattern needs a stop and ranks, or no pattern, as the notes say), and its beam that hops between up to four air targets, paid in energy (weapon trait chain; resource energy); its description was rewritten in July 2026.
keep.why: An economy that flies and fights: the enemy hunts it to starve the side of power. The data's Hacker must stop to earn and the kept Overlord raises the cap instead; earning on the move is new.

keep.brief: Nyx (shared; Advanced Vehicle Factory, t2, 500 metal, low; added in the June 2025 update): cover the unarmed truck with a wide mobile radar and a short-range radar jammer, both always on (sensor traits radar and jammer, so no jam-sensors), and its running cost of 700 energy a second from the side's pool.
keep.why: The first radar in the data: enemy blips far beyond sight for the whole team. Its jammer overlaps the kept MechWarrior Raven's ECM bubble; the radar and the energy upkeep are what it adds.

keep.brief: Locusts (shared, added in TITANS; Advanced Bot Factory or Unit Cannon, t2, 500 metal, low): cover the very fast hovering nanobot swarm that skims land, water and lava (speed 30 against the Dox's 20), the short beam that hits ten times a second and is aimed at metal (family nanites), its 160 health, and no wreck by its blueprint (an uncertain entry, as the game notes say); settle from a source what eating metal does, for example whether it pays the owner (deconstruct-target, proposed); if no page says, add an uncertain entry and code a plain beam.
keep.why: A swarm that eats a base rather than shooting it, and the first nanites weapon in the data. The kept Zergling is a cheap, fast swarm too but bites rather than strips; crossing lava and the deconstruction are new.

keep.brief: Raven RVN-3L (Liao, light, 35 t): cover the Guardian ECM bubble that hides teammates near it and spoils enemy locks (an always-on ECM is the jammer trait by the notes, and MechWarrior Online's key only switches it to a counter mode, so settle jam-sensors against the trait from current patch notes), the Beagle probe, TAG and Narc (the weapon trait mark by the granularity rule; mark-target only if coded as abilities) and its light guns; counters: probes, TAG from outside the bubble and destroying the torso that holds the suite; stealth armour is only on the RVN-4L (notes).
keep.why: Electronic warfare as a whole job, and the registry's jam-sensors example (MechWarrior Online's Guardian ECM). The kept StarCraft II Raven lowers armour; this one hides allies and marks targets for missiles. It pairs with the kept Catapult.

keep.brief: Firestarter FS9-H (Inner Sphere, light, 35 t): cover the four flamers (one firing backwards from the centre torso), two medium lasers, two machine guns and six jump jets (leap), and flamers that heat a 'Mech up rather than hurt it much, kill infantry and set woods alight; link stack-to-overload through its heat-to-shutdown variant, which already names this weapon, and check whether MechWarrior Online still stops flamer heat short of a shutdown.
keep.why: A weapon that attacks the enemy's heat rather than its armour: the registry's heat-to-shutdown example. Its flamers and machine guns are also the batch's answer to the kept Elemental.

keep.brief: Hatchetman HCT-3F (Steiner, medium, 45 t): cover the AC/10, two medium lasers, four jump jets (leap) and the hatchet (family blades, delivery melee; it outhits a punch and adds no heat), while the game-wide punches and kicks stay off, and the full-head ejection system, which blasts the whole head clear as an escape pod that usually steers toward friends (on_death pilot-eject, with the flight in notes).
keep.why: A carried melee weapon on a 'Mech and a head that flies to safety: two memorable twists for a player.

keep.brief: Phoenix Hawk LAM PHX-HK2 (Inner Sphere, medium, 50 t, tabletop only): cover the three forms, 'Mech, AirMech (low flight in ground effect) and aerospace fighter with limited fuel (transform; a card holds one mode, so record the third form in notes and report the limit as a rule problem), hits to limb actuators, hips or gyro that can jam the conversion (transform, jammed-conversion variant), and its guns (one large laser, a pair of medium lasers and twin machine guns); its play fields rest on proposals.
keep.why: The registry's jammed-conversion example and MechWarrior's only flying form. Its ground-and-air switch overlaps the kept Viking; the third form and the jam that damage causes are what it adds.

keep.brief: Catapult CPLT-C1 (Liao, heavy, 65 t): cover the two LRM-15 racks that lock on and, in MechWarrior Online, fire indirectly at targets teammates share, with a minimum range and few reloads (resource limited-ammo), the four medium lasers for anything inside that range, four jump jets (leap), and no arms or anti-infantry guns; counters: an ECM bubble and a light 'Mech that gets inside the minimum range; team-play hook spotter, with the Raven.
keep.why: Missile fire support that needs a teammate's lock. It overlaps the kept Siege Tank's need for spotters and its dead zone; the lock-on that ECM breaks, which ties it to the Raven, is what it adds. The batch's heavy 'Mech.

keep.brief: Atlas AS7-D (Inner Sphere or shared, as the faction rules decide: every Great House fields it and Clans refit captured ones; assault, 100 t): cover the slow juggernaut's AC/20, an LRM-20 that fires directly or indirectly, an SRM-6 and four medium lasers, two of them facing backwards to punish flankers, and the skull-like head shaped to frighten (memorable); the command variant goes in notes.
keep.why: Rear-facing guns as the answer to circling, on BattleTech's best-known boss 'Mech.

keep.brief: Executioner (Gladiator) Prime (Clan OmniMech, assault, 95 t): cover MASC, short sprints from 64.8 to 86.4 km/h whose overuse damages or locks the leg actuators (overclock-self, slump-after variant), four fixed jump jets (leap), the Gauss rifle and two ER large lasers, and the old MechWarrior Online wiki's claim that the Gauss rifle explodes when destroyed (check current patch notes); its pod configurations are loadout picks.
keep.why: The registry's slump-after example: a boost whose cost lands on the legs, on an assault frame. The kept Marine pays health and the Void Ray pays speed; this one risks its own legs.

keep.brief: Dire Wolf (Daishi) Prime (Clan OmniMech, assault, 100 t): cover four ER large lasers, four medium pulse lasers, an LRM-10 and two Ultra AC/5s that fire at double rate, burning ammunition and heat faster, with a chance in MechWarrior Online that each double shot jams the gun for a few seconds (double-tap-jam, proposed, or a weapon trait), and its pilot rationing fire to stay cool; check the jam figures against current patch notes.
keep.why: A fire-rate gamble the data does not have. It repeats the kept Atlas as a slow juggernaut; the Ultra autocannon jam is what it adds.

keep.brief: Elemental (Clan battle armour, a squad): cover each suit's 90 m jump (leap), the missile pack it drops once empty, and the battle claw that rips armour or grips an OmniMech; in MechWarrior 5: Clans' Flash Storm DLC, enemy Points leap onto a 'Mech and cling to it to hurt it (infest-vehicle) while friendly Points finish a 'Mech whose head armour is gone (execute-target) and come back a while after being wiped out (reinforce-squad); and riding friendly OmniMechs on handholds that open to a friendly signal, six suits to a 'Mech (ride-on-ally, proposed); anti-personnel weapons are its counter.
keep.why: The anti-'Mech squad and the batch's only infantry outside StarCraft II and the Halo games. Latching on repeats the data's Terror Drone, a drone; this squad also rides friends and finishes a stripped 'Mech.

cut.reason: Same line as the kept Halo Wars 2 Jerome-092. Halopedia's Red Team page says the Halo Wars 2 Spartans act almost as in Halo Wars but add the EMP hold, the Spartan Slam and a takeover cancelled by death, so the line stays in Halo Wars 2; this version's extras (three per army, outside the population cap) go in Jerome's notes.

Its EMP that stops a vehicle from firing repeats the kept StarCraft II Raven's Interference Matrix (disable-machine, weapons-lock variant) and the data's Terror Drone, and the chain upgrade is the trait the Voltaic Tank already has. It is Anders' only unique unit, so Halo Wars keeps the units of two of its three UNSC leaders.

Overdrive spends its shield on beam damage, one more cost for overclock-self, which the kept Marine, Void Ray, Arbiter and Executioner already carry, and standing still to fire repeats the kept Siege Tank's and Lurker's stop-to-fight lesson; fire-when-stopped is not proposed from this batch. Halo Wars 2's Locust is the same line without Overdrive.

Its lockdown into long-range artillery repeats the kept Siege Tank (deploy-siege-mode is the data's most used pattern), and its piercing railgun rounds are a weapon trait. deploy-siege-mode's pattern file names it as an example, but that id is well covered.
A cheap shielded rifleman that links no pattern: its gauntlet shield is an armour model and its anti-infantry job is common in the data.

Same line as the kept Halo Wars 2 Scarab, which adds the plasma-shield invulnerability, Thrasher missiles and Skitterer riders; the Halo Wars cap of two goes in that entry's notes. Cutting it leaves Halo Wars with no tier-3 unit, since it was the game's only tier-3 candidate.

A slow flying fortress with a slow power shot repeats the kept Battlecruiser (capital ship, fire-power-shot); its dodgeable shells are a weakness note. The kept Scarab already fills Halo Wars 2's super-unit tier.

Its two escort Sentinels repeat launch-drones (the kept Swarm Host and Jackrabbit, and the kept Prophet of Regret, whose escorts are this same Sentinel), its stun bolt is a weapon trait and its slowing death pulse an on_death note.

Its healing repeats the kept Medivac, and its stacking shield, which Halopedia's Info line says cuts the damage taken inside it, repeats the kept Sentry's Guardian Shield and Infestor's Microbial Shroud; the kept Immortal already carries raise-shield. Halo Wars' Huragok is the same line, so neither game keeps it.

His paint that slows enemies and strips their armour repeats the kept StarCraft II Raven's armour-lowering missile and the MechWarrior Raven's TAG (mark-target); his reflecting shield repeats retaliate-on-hit, and his structure repair and healing drones repeat repair-allies and launch-drones.

His gravity pull repeats the kept Viper's Abduct and Phoenix's lift (pull-target), and he is the same hammer-brute line as the kept Halo Wars Brute Chieftain, whose vortex teaches more; heal-on-hit is on the kept Hunter Captain.

Repairs, mines and teleporters repeat the data's Iron Harvest Engineer, the kept Widow Mine and the kept Commander, which builds teleporters too (build-linked-exits); its mine sight is a detector fit note.

A long-range sniper repeats the data's Jarmen Kell and the kept Ghost and Tempest, and its beam that downs missiles repeats the kept Shroud's point defence. First swap if Planetary Annihilation needs a medium-price unit or a marksman.
A hover gunboat from the naval yard teaches little beyond its class and terrain, and hover is already common in the data and in this batch. First swap if a high-price or naval-yard unit is wanted.
Its repair aura repeats the kept Medivac, its reclaim repeats gather-resources (the kept Commander reclaims), and its beam that downs missiles repeats the kept Shroud's point defence.

A flying far end of the team's teleporter repeats the kept Warp Prism's forward arrival point and the data's Thunderhead (build-linked-exits); the kept SXX-1304 already teaches the orbital layer and the kept Atlas the titan tier.

Its anti-infantry machine guns repeat the kept Firestarter's job and a weapon common in the data, and its rear-armour hunting and component wrecking lean on armour rules that are game-wide for every 'Mech. First swap if a very fast light raider or a dedicated counter to the Elemental is wanted.
Firepower capped by heat is game-wide (every 'Mech uses the heat resource), so it adds a strengths-and-weaknesses note rather than a mechanic.

Tabletop only; four legs are already in the data (Iron Harvest walkers, the Sickle), its solid-or-cluster ammunition switch repeats switch-weapon-mode (the kept Thor), and its fixed torso with a sidestep is a word-list gap for the rule-fix round.
Iconic, but its pod configurations are loadout picks that every kept OmniMech (Executioner, Dire Wolf) carries too, and its LRMs repeat the kept Catapult.

Tabletop only, and its cooling of overheated 'Mechs exists only in design text with no game rule, so no source shows how it plays. Cutting it leaves House Kurita and a MechWarrior vehicle uncovered; first swap if the generator wants a heat-support partner for the Firestarter.

opening_reason: No opening check is planned, and none is needed by the plan's line: with no rule change between R3 and R4, R4 needs none. The runbook's own test, git log 48629b8..HEAD over data/vocab, schemas, scripts/build-docs.mjs and scripts/validate.mjs (48629b8 holds R3's agreement report), prints one commit, 2d94131. It only describes the games registry's status field, a schema wording Mustafa approved on 11 November 2026 as no rule change, so no rule for a unit's fields has changed. If a check is run anyway, take the Siege Tank (StarCraft II) and the Raven RVN-3L (MechWarrior/BattleTech). They come from the two rule systems that differ most, which together hold 58 of the batch's 85 units, and neither needs a new pattern, so a split points at the word lists or the new game notes. The Siege Tank tests the two-resource price at the anchor itself (525), attribute bonuses in the roles rule, a second form in modes[], the min-range and friendly-fire traits, and a reach longer than its sight. The Raven tests MechWarrior's heat resource, zonal and directional armour, a light 'Mech in the armour map, the torso-twist mount tie-break, the line between always on and on a key for its ECM (the jammer trait or jam-sensors), and the granularity rule for TAG and Narc (the weapon trait mark or mark-target). Coder briefs, name only: 'Siege Tank (Terran, StarCraft II: Legacy of the Void)' and 'Raven RVN-3L (House Liao, MechWarrior / BattleTech)'.
coverage:
KEPT: 85 units. StarCraft II 49 (Terran 15, Zerg 16, Protoss 18): every Legacy of the Void multiplayer unit but the three workers, with no trim. Halo Wars 9, Halo Wars 2 9, Planetary Annihilation: TITANS 9 and MechWarrior/BattleTech 9, so 36, as asked. The plan said about 86; it is 85 because the Hellbat is a mode of the Hellion. CUT: 21, each with a reason. None of the four smaller games had a unit in data/units before.

STARCRAFT II LIST: complete, and nothing added. Checked against the plan's closed list and the researcher's roster note: the workers, the MULE, the Larva and the Cocoon are out; the Changeling, Locust, Broodling and Interceptor are coded with the Overseer, Swarm Host, Brood Lord and Carrier; what patches removed (the Mothership Core in 4.0, the Infestor's infested terrans in 4.11.0, the Raven's older abilities) stays out; the Auto-Turret, Stasis Ward, Creep Tumor, Adept shade, hallucinations and Purification Nova belong to their makers; the Nydus Worm, the crawlers and the Terran buildings that lift off are structures. No unit is missing. One split question: the Hellion and the Hellbat stay one entry (sc2.terran.hellion) by the modes rule in docs/fields.md, since the switch changes how the unit moves and what it is, and a unit that can be built in either form takes as its base the form whose name it carries (the shared button is Hellion Transformation). I agree with the researcher; if Mustafa wants the Hellbat as an entry of its own, the count becomes 50. No other split: the Viking, Siege Tank, Liberator, Thor, Observer and Overseer keep their second forms as modes, and the Baneling, Ravager, Lurker, Overseer, Brood Lord and Archon are units of their own, as the plan says.

HALO LINES KEPT ONCE: the Spartan stays in Halo Wars 2 as Jerome-092 (Halopedia's Red Team page, Halo Wars 2 section and its list of changes from Halo Wars: the EMP hold, the Spartan Slam and a takeover cancelled by death come on top of the old boarding), and the Scarab stays in Halo Wars 2 (shield and riders added). The Arbiter, Banshee, Ghost, Hunter pair and Cyclops stay in Halo Wars, whose versions keep the running cost, the dive, the Strafe, the bond and the repair kit that their Halo Wars 2 versions lack (none of those was a Halo Wars 2 candidate). The Huragok is cut in both games. The hammer Brute stays in Halo Wars (the Chieftain) and Decimus's Warlord is cut. Kinsano's Cyclops shares only the suit with Halo Wars' Cyclops, and the Hunter Captain is a hero rather than the bonded pair, so both are separate units with separate lessons.

REPEATS WITH STARCRAFT II: cut because a StarCraft II unit already teaches the lesson: Gremlin (the Raven's Interference Matrix), Cobra (Siege Tank), Locust (the Void Ray's power mode and the stop-to-fire deploys), Condor (Battlecruiser), the Halo Wars 2 Engineer (the Sentry's Guardian Shield and the Medivac's healing), Pavium (the Raven's armour-lowering missile), Warlord (the Viper's Abduct), Protector Sentinel (Swarm Host, Carrier), Helios (Warp Prism), Angel (Medivac), Gil-E (Ghost, Tempest) and Barghest (the Thor's mode switch). Kept despite an overlap, each for the twist it adds: Elephant (Warp Prism; it trains units from a ground hull), Arbiter (Stimpack and Dark Templar; paid by the team's money), Prophet of Regret (Disruptor; a held beam), Brute Chieftain (Viper and Psionic Storm; the release blast), Banshee (Baneling; a dive set off by low health), Ghost (the Zealot's charge; the dodge), Cyclops (Medivac and Queen repairs; melee demolition), Jackrabbit (Swarm Host; one helper drone bought as an add-on), Kinsano's Cyclops (Psionic Storm; a line of fire), Colossus (Thor; Stomp), Shroud (the Mothership's cloak; point defence and the forced choice), Methane Wagon (Guardian Shield; the enemy debuff), Scarab (the StarCraft II Colossus's cliff walking; the shield and the super-unit tier), Commander (Yamato; king piece and builder), Manhattan (Baneling; a death that hurts both sides), Astraeus (Medivac and Warp Prism; travel between worlds), Icarus (Overlord; income on the move), Locusts (Zergling; deconstruction and lava), Catapult (Siege Tank; locks that ECM breaks), Executioner (Stimpack; the cost on its legs), the MechWarrior Raven (the StarCraft II Raven's mark; ECM), Phoenix Hawk LAM (Viking; the third form and the jam) and Hatchetman (Zealot and Ultralisk melee; the hatchet and the head pod). Repeats between the four smaller games: the ground slam (the Colossus on a key, the Atlas as its weapon, Jerome-092 when he lands to board) and riding an ally (Skitterer, Elemental), each counted as one proposed id; the jammer (Nyx and the MechWarrior Raven: radar and upkeep on one side, marking and counter-ECM on the other); point defence for allies kept once (Shroud; the Angel and Gil-E cut).

CLASSES (the candidates' guesses; the fill settles them): infantry 24 (17 of them StarCraft II, Zerg beasts counted as infantry), aircraft 24, walker 20 (eight 'Mechs and three Planetary Annihilation bots among them), vehicle 8, hover 5, drone 4. Air layers: StarCraft II's fliers share one layer in the game, so the fill sets low or high air by the rules; the SXX-1304 and the Astraeus fly in orbit, a layer the word lists lack (aircraft with fit notes); the LAM's fighter form is the only jet among the four smaller games. No ships: none of StarCraft II and the two Halo Wars games builds one, the Planetary Annihilation researcher offered none (its ships repeat a carrier, a submarine and artillery) and MechWarrior's naval units were left out, so the data keeps only RA1's Submarine. Odd ones: the merged Archon and the morphs, the king-piece Commander, two orbital units, a nanobot swarm, the Skitterer (a worm colony that rides allies), the bonded Hunter pair, a battle armour squad, the three-form LAM and the unarmed casters and supports (Raven, Infestor, Viper, Disruptor, Shroud, Nyx, Astraeus).

FACTIONS: StarCraft II Terran 15, Zerg 16, Protoss 18. Halo Wars UNSC 2 (the Elephant for Cutter, the Cyclops for Forge; Anders' Gremlin cut) and Covenant 7 (all three leaders). Halo Wars 2 UNSC 4 (Jerome-092 for Cutter, Kinsano's Cyclops, Johnson's Colossus, the Jackrabbit) and Banished 5 (Colony's Skitterer and Hunter Captain, Yapyap's Methane Wagon, the Scarab, the Shroud); the Flood is AI only. Planetary Annihilation shared 9 (one roster). MechWarrior: Inner Sphere 3 (Firestarter, LAM, and the Atlas, which may be shared), Liao 2 (Raven, Catapult), Steiner 1 (Hatchetman), Clan 3 (Executioner, Dire Wolf, Elemental); Kurita goes with the cut Coolant Truck, and Davion and Marik had no candidate.

TIERS: StarCraft II t1 13, t2 23, t3 13 by the registry gates. Halo Wars, by the drafted registry entry (tech 0 is t1, tech 1 and 2 are t2, the Temple leaders t2): t1 2 (Elephant, Ghost), t2 7, and no t3, because its only tier-3 candidate, the Scarab, is kept in the sequel. Halo Wars 2: t1 6, t2 1 (Shroud), t3 2 (Colossus, Scarab). Planetary Annihilation: t1 3 (Commander, Astraeus, Icarus), t2 5, t3 1 (Atlas). MechWarrior has no tiers or prices; weight classes stand in: light 2 (Raven, Firestarter), medium 2 (Hatchetman, LAM), heavy 1 (Catapult), assault 3 (Atlas, Executioner, Dire Wolf), and the battle armour.

PRICE BANDS: StarCraft II, the researcher's count, to be checked at 5.0.17: very low 15, low 12, medium 13, high 5, very high 4. Halo Wars, by the drafted supplies thresholds: very low 3 (Cyclops, Banshee, Ghost), low 2 (Vampire, Hunter), medium 4 (the Elephant, and the three leaders at 400, who first arrive free), nothing higher (only the cut Scarab and the Vulture sit there). ROLES (primary guesses): StarCraft II covers assault, anti-armour, anti-infantry, anti-air, siege, raider, scout, support, transport, disabler, area-denial, buffer and infiltrator. The four smaller games add engineer (the Commander, and the Elephant as a second role) and logistics (Icarus), with more siege (Cyclops, Prophet of Regret, SXX-1304, Bluehawk, Manhattan, Catapult), scouts (Ghost, Jackrabbit, Skitterer, Nyx, the MechWarrior Raven), buffers (Shroud, Methane Wagon) and raiders (Locusts, LAM). No marksman primary is kept (the cut Gil-E was the candidate); the data already has two.

new_patterns.summary: On a key, lock your guns onto one enemy; they keep firing by themselves while you move freely, until a timer runs out or the target escapes a leash range, so the fight is about staying close rather than aiming.

Hit one enemy or an area so its ability energy drains away (in some versions its energy shields too), leaving casters unable to cast until it builds back; some versions turn the drained energy into damage.
Two units fuse into one stronger unit that keeps their combined price; for players, two teammates could pool into one shared body. patterns.md had left the Archon merge out for want of examples.
Plant or drip a growth that spreads over time into ground where your side moves faster and can see, and which enemies must find and clear. patterns.md had left StarCraft II creep out for now.
Target a friendly production building so it turns out extra units for a while; in a shooter, faster respawns or extra spawn slots at a base.

Just by staying alive you raise your team's unit cap; when you die the team cannot add units until you are replaced, so enemies hunt you to stall the side. The Icarus's energy income while alive is a cousin that the Planetary Annihilation notes send to generate-income with a fit note.
From range, slime or jam an enemy building so it cannot produce or research for a while, without damaging it; close to capture-structure's sabotage variant, which works from inside.

On a key, net an area: enemies in it are badly slowed and hurt for a few seconds, cannot blink, jump, burrow or board, and hidden ones show. patterns.md folds plain roots and slows into weapon traits, so the ability version and the blocked escapes are the new part.
Hold a spray or beam on one target; its damage climbs the longer it stays on and resets when you break off (the ability form of the charge-up trait).

Draw health from a friendly building to refill your own ability energy, so energy is bought with the team's repairs. The nearest id is sacrifice-for-allies through its feed-the-caster variant (Brood War's Consume); the merge pass may fold it there.
Release a slow orb and steer it for a moment before it bursts, hurting everything near it, friends included; enemies who watch it can scatter. It may fold into fire-power-shot as a variant.

Call a beam down from above and drive it by hand over ground you can see; it burns everything under it, your own side included but never you, for as long as you keep it up. A held cousin of steer-delayed-blast: the merge pass may join the two.
Your weapon works only while switched on and drains energy every second; switch it off to bank energy for your other abilities. It may be a resource rule rather than a pattern.
An ability runs only while the team's shared money pays for it every second, so power is bought with the team's economy. It may fit better as a resource term than as a pattern.
Hold up a spinning field that drags enemies close and grinds them; ending it, or having it cut short, sets off a last blast, so the skill lies in timing the release.
An enemy finished off by your draining attack bursts when it dies and hurts everything around it, so a kill inside a tight formation spreads damage to its neighbours.
Two units fielded as a bonded pair hit much harder while both live; when one dies the survivor loses the bonus and becomes easier prey. band-together counts a nearby group, not one named partner.

Slam the ground so every enemy ground unit in a ring around you is hit, and in some versions stunned: on a key (the Colossus's Stomp; the stun when the Spartan Slam lands on a vehicle to board it) or as a unit's only weapon on a cycle (the Atlas, which may instead be the radial aim model with no pattern). Folds the proposals ground-slam and stomp-shockwave.

Cling to the outside of a friendly vehicle or walker and ride it: in one version you keep firing, add to its health and die only with it, and the host's size sets how many fit (the Skitterer); in another you are carried exposed into battle and jump off to fight (the Elemental). join-ally-crew boards inside, one rider per vehicle. Folds the proposals latch-onto-ally and ride-on-ally.
An always-on cloud around you makes your own troops of one kind hit harder and take less damage while enemies inside it hit softer and lose armour; shells you fire start the same cloud elsewhere.

An automatic point defence shoots down a few incoming shells and missiles aimed at you or at teammates near you; a volley bigger than it can handle gets through. The interceptor armour model guards only its owner. Folds the proposals point-defence-allies and intercept-for-allies; the cut Angel and Gil-E were the other examples.
The side's survival rides on one unit: when it dies, its player is out, so enemies hunt it and teammates guard it. The game notes may call this a game-mode rule instead.
A short-range swarm beam strips a unit or building down instead of blasting it; in some versions the stripped material pays your side (not yet sourced for the Locusts).
An automatic weapon fires at enemy units while they are being launched or dropped in, killing them before they land (to confirm on PA Lobby's Unit Cannon page).
Leave the current planet or arena under your own power, with any cargo, and arrive on another; only units marked as interplanetary can.
Hold a separate layer above the fight that only anti-orbit weapons reach, and fire straight down at what lies beneath; as much a word-list gap (no orbital mobility or target type) as a pattern.
Fire a weapon at double rate when you choose, accepting a chance that it jams and falls silent for a few seconds. It may belong in the weapon traits rather than the patterns.
